title: CORS misconfigurations and clickjacking
summary: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy, so a bad policy hands your users' data to any site. Spot origin reflection with credentials and the null origin, write an exact allow-list, and stop framing with frame-ancestors.

steps.title: The misconfiguration in two headers
body: By default a script on `evil.example` may send a request to `api.shop.example`, but may **not read** the answer. CORS headers are the API saying "this origin may read me":

The server **reflected** whatever `Origin` it received and allowed credentials. Now any site the victim visits can `fetch('https://api.shop.example/api/me', { credentials: 'include' })` and read their data. In ASP.NET Core that is `SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true).AllowCredentials()`. (`AllowAnyOrigin().AllowCredentials()` is refused by ASP.NET Core at start-up, and browsers ignore `*` with credentials, which is why people reach for the reflection instead.)

Other classics: `Origin: null` allowed (sandboxed iframes and `file:` pages send `null`, and attackers can produce it on purpose), and prefix or suffix checks: `origin.EndsWith("shop.example")` allows `evilshop.example`; `StartsWith("https://app.shop.example")` allows `https://app.shop.example.evil.example`.

steps.prompt: The API allows credentials. Which `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` policies are safe?
Someone says: "CORS is our API's security: only our SPA's origin is allowed." Which is true?
options: CORS only controls what browsers let other sites' scripts read; curl and servers ignore it, so the API still needs authentication and authorization
Right: requests from other origins are blocked by the server
Right, as long as preflight caching is off
CORS also stops CSRF, so no antiforgery tokens are needed
steps.explain: CORS is a browser relaxation of the same-origin policy, not an access control. And a simple cross-site POST is sent without any preflight, so CORS does not stop CSRF either.

steps.title: Clickjacking: your page, invisible, under their button
body: An attacker's page loads your **Delete my account** page in an invisible `<iframe>` and puts a "Win a lamp!" button exactly over your real button. The user clicks theirs and presses yours, signed in.
The defence is a header that says who may frame you:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'          (or 'self', or a list of origins)
X-Frame-Options: DENY                                    (the older header, for old browsers)

`frame-ancestors` only works as a **header**, not in a `<meta>` tag. Send both headers on every HTML response; SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies also mean a cross-site iframe arrives signed out, which helps.

steps.prompt: Match each header to what it controls.
pairs: which other origins' scripts may read the response
whether that read may include cookies
no site may put this page in a frame

steps.title: An exact CORS allow-list, and no framing
prompt: 1. The CORS policy `spa` allows **only** `https://app.shop.example`, with credentials, methods `GET` and `PUT`, and the header `content-type`. Any other origin (including `null` and look-alikes) gets no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
2. Every response carries `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (a small middleware).
**Run checks** sends real CORS requests and preflights with different `Origin` headers.
hints: Replace `SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true)` with `WithOrigins("https://app.shop.example")`, and the `AllowAny...` calls with `WithMethods("GET", "PUT")` and `WithHeaders("content-type")`.
The framing headers: `ctx.Response.Headers.ContentSecurityPolicy = "frame-ancestors 'none'"; ctx.Response.Headers.XFrameOptions = "DENY";` in an `app.Use(...)` middleware.
template: {{CODE}}
static class DojoTests
static async Task<HttpResponseMessage> Get(HttpClient http, string origin)
var msg = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get, "/api/me");
msg.Headers.Add("Origin", origin);
return await http.SendAsync(msg);
static string? Acao(HttpResponseMessage r) => r.Headers.TryGetValues("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", out var v) ? v.First() : null;
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("CORS could be checked", async () =>
var ok = await Get(http, "https://app.shop.example");
Dojo.Eq("the SPA's origin is allowed, exactly", "https://app.shop.example", Acao(ok));
Dojo.Eq("...with credentials", "true", ok.Headers.TryGetValues("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", out var c) ? c.First() : null);
Dojo.Eq("https://evil.example is not allowed", null, Acao(await Get(http, "https://evil.example")));
Dojo.Eq("the null origin is not allowed", null, Acao(await Get(http, "null")));
Dojo.Eq("a look-alike suffix is not allowed", null, Acao(await Get(http, "https://app.shop.example.evil.example")));
Dojo.Eq("http (not https) is not allowed", null, Acao(await Get(http, "http://app.shop.example")));
var pre = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Options, "/api/me");
pre.Headers.Add("Origin", "https://app.shop.example");
pre.Headers.Add("Access-Control-Request-Method", "PUT");
pre.Headers.Add("Access-Control-Request-Headers", "content-type");
Dojo.Eq("a preflight for PUT from the SPA is allowed", "https://app.shop.example", Acao(await http.SendAsync(pre)));
var bad = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Options, "/api/me");
bad.Headers.Add("Origin", "https://evil.example");
bad.Headers.Add("Access-Control-Request-Method", "PUT");
Dojo.Eq("a preflight from evil.example is not allowed", null, Acao(await http.SendAsync(bad)));
await Dojo.TryAsync("Framing could be checked", async () =>
var r = await http.GetAsync("/account");
var csp = r.Headers.TryGetValues("Content-Security-Policy", out var v) ? string.Join(";", v) : "";
Dojo.Check("the account page says frame-ancestors 'none'", csp.Contains("frame-ancestors 'none'"), csp);
Dojo.Eq("...and X-Frame-Options: DENY", "DENY", r.Headers.TryGetValues("X-Frame-Options", out var x) ? x.First() : null);
